pass_a_gloss: For we seek whether, as the anger of all is evil but God’s is refuting, and the wrath of all is harsh but the so-called wrath of God is educative, and the regret of all of us accuses weakness of the one before the regret, but upon God his regret does not accuse God but the outward affairs upon which the regret is taken—so also one must understand the deception of God as of another kind beside our deception with which we deceive. What then is the deception beside God’s, which the prophet understood, when he ceased being deceived, and says, knowing the benefit from having been deceived: 'You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived'? And first I will use a Hebrew tradition that has come to us through someone who fled because of the faith of Christ and because of having gone up from the law and having come where we spend time. He told either a story that appears or a word able to lead the hearers to 'You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived.' He said such things: God does not tyrannize but reigns, and reigning he does not force but persuades, and wants those under him to offer themselves willingly to his economy, that the good of someone may not be according to necessity but according to his willing. Which Paul also knowing said in the letter to Philemon to Philemon about Onesimus: 'that your good may not be according to necessity but according to willing.' The God of all could then make a supposed good in us, that of necessity we give alms and of necessity be temperate, but he has not wished it. Therefore he does not command us to do what we do from grief or from necessity, that what comes to be may be willing. He seeks a way, so to speak, how someone may willingly do what God wants. The tradition then also told me something such: he wanted to send Jeremiah to prophesy to all the nations and before all the nations to the people. But since the prophecies had something more gloomy—for they announced punishments which each according to worth will be punished—and he knew the prophet’s choice not wanting to prophesy the worse things to the people of Israel, for this reason he managed to say: 'Take this cup, and you will make all the nations drink to whom I will send you.' God then commanded Jeremiah to take a cup, and urging him upon taking the cup of the unmixed wine he says: 'And I will send you to all the nations having this cup of the unmixed wine.' And Jeremiah hearing that he is sent to all the nations, that he will serve them a cup of wrath, a cup of punishments, not suspecting that Israel also is about to drink from the cup of punishment, was deceived…

pass_b_english: For we seek whether, as everyone’s anger is evil but God’s is refuting, and everyone’s wrath is harsh but God’s so-called wrath is educative, and our regret accuses weakness in the one before the regret, but upon God his regret does not accuse God but the outward affairs upon which the regret is taken—so also one must understand the deception of God as of another kind beside our deception with which we deceive. What then is the deception beside God’s, which the prophet understood when he ceased being deceived, and says, knowing the benefit from having been deceived: 'You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived' (Jeremiah 20:7)?

And first I will use a Hebrew tradition that has come to us through someone who fled because of the faith of Christ and because of having gone up from the law and having come where we spend time. He told either a story that appears or a word able to lead the hearers to 'You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived.' (Isaiah 6:8) He said such things: God does not tyrannize but reigns, and reigning he does not force but persuades, and wants those under him to offer themselves willingly to his economy, that someone’s good may not be according to necessity but according to the willing. Which Paul also knowing said in the letter to Philemon about Onesimus: 'that your good may not be according to necessity but according to willing.' (Isaiah 6:9–10) The God of all could then make a supposed good in us, that of necessity we give alms and of necessity be temperate, but he has not wished it. Therefore he does not command us to do what we do from grief or from necessity, that what comes to be may be willing. He seeks a way, so to speak, how someone may willingly do what God wants.

The tradition then also told me something such: he wanted to send Jeremiah to prophesy to all the nations and before all the nations to the people. But since the prophecies had something more gloomy—for they announced punishments which each according to worth will be punished—and he knew the prophet’s choice not wanting to prophesy the worse things to the people of Israel, for this reason he managed to say: 'Take this cup, and you will make all the nations drink to whom I will send you.' (Jeremiah 4:7 or Hos 5:14 (lion imagery)) God then commanded Jeremiah to take a cup, and urging him upon taking the cup of the unmixed wine he says he will send him to all the nations having this cup. And Jeremiah hearing that he is sent to all the nations to serve a cup of wrath, a cup of punishments, not suspecting that Israel also is about to drink from the cup of punishment, was deceived.
